pr_title: kernel: add new work queue implementation
pr_body:
This PR replaces #28891 as a candidate solution for  #27356 by addressing the concerns identified in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/28891#issuecomment-711024794.

It provides a complete reimplementation of the work queue infrastructure intended to eliminate the race conditions and feature gaps in the existing implementation.  The general functionality is based on that provided by Linux.

Both bare and delayable work structures are supported.  Items can be submitted; delayable items can be scheduled for submission at a future time.  Items can be delayed, queued, and running all at the same time. A running item can also be canceling.

The new implementation:
* replaces "pending" with "busy" which identifies the active states;
* supports canceling delayed and submitted items;
* prevents resubmission of a item being canceled until cancellation   completes;
* supports waiting for cancellation to complete;
* supports flushing a work item (waiting for the last submission to complete without preventing resubmission);
* supports waiting for a queue to drain (only allows resubmission from the work thread);
* prevents handler-reentrancy during resubmission.

Details on the API changes are in [this comment](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/29618#issuecomment-738139695).

Fixes #27356

### Plan for Merge

There is a strong desire to get this in to 2.5 so that the legacy API could be removed for 2.6 (LTS) if TSC approves an exception. IIRC discussion off-line suggested that this API could be restricted to supervisory mode use, however there is a large open question regarding how/whether user mode needs a similar capability.

Current steps required to merge this (**rm DRAFT** are conditions that block removing the DNM status from this)

* [x] Remove the old implementation (currently unselected by Kconfig): **NOTE** This causes massive irrelevant changes to be observed in the start to finish diff of `include/kernel.h`.  See the individual commits to confirm that only the old API was removed.
* [x] Document which parts of the legacy API will remain, and which parts are to be deprecated.  See [this comment](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/29618#issuecomment-738139695).
* [x] Full test and code coverage
* [x] Determine the degree to which `k_work_submit_to_user_queue` must be supported.  (Needs input from out-of-tree users: Zephyr itself does not use it).  **RESOLUTION**: provide new API with the same function names and behavior, but different signatures since `k_work` and `k_workq` cannot be shared between supervisor and userspace interfaces.)
* [x] If necessary, provide a deprecated work around for legacy user queue API.  **RESOLUTION** Not applicable; the replacement API will not be backward compatible in signature, but will be compatible in implementation.
* [x] Determine whether #29668 is going anywhere and finalize the method for handling scheduling in the implementation.  **RESOLUTION**: Extracted the used functions as kernel private functions until we confirm they're suitable for public exposure.
* [x] Pass CI on all platforms (confirmed possible)
* [x] Confirm that deprecated usages in-tree (largely networking and bluetooth) can be successfully replaced by the new API, probably via draft PRs based on this PR.

For posterity here are the design notes prior to implementation, which may provide some high-level insight of intent.  The material is obsolete as implementation often identified a better path or desired behavior.

<details><summary>Expand for content</summary>

Design questions:
* Is there a need to be able to dynamically create and destroy workqueue objects and threads?  Absent compelling justification the answer is "no".

## Queue States and Actions

Design requirements:
* It must be possible to drain a work queue in the sense of [Linux drain_workqueue](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/workqueue.html#c.drain_workqueue).

* It must be possible to flush a work queue in the sense of [Linux flush_workqueue](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/workqueue.html#c.flush_workqueue).

### Terminology

*chained work* is work that is submitted from a work queue thread to the same work queue.

### States

A queue has a *lock* that protects the other members of the state.

A queue has a *work list* which is a sequence of items to be processed.

A queue has a *drain waitq* that holds threads that are waiting for it to drain.

A queue has a set of *flags* including:
* *draining* which indicates that it has been instructed accept only chained work.

### Actions

A *submit* action [any] provides an item.  It is invoked when the global
work item lock is held.  Atomically:
* If the queue is not draining or the work item is chained:
  * the item is added to the work list;
  * the work item queued bit is set;
  * the work thread is notified
The action result indicates whether the inner actions were taken.

A *cancel* action [external] provides an item.  It is invoked when the global work item lock is held.  Atomically:
* If the item is removed from the queue:
  * the work item queued bit is cleared;
  * the work thread is notified

A *check* action [internal] is invoked whenever the work thread is notified or completes a process action.  Atomically:
* Any pending notification is cleared.
* If no work item is available:
  * if the queue is draining the drain waitq is woken
* If a work item is fetched then:
  * the work item queued bit is cleared;
  * the work item running bit is set;
The lock is released.  If a work item was fetched a process action is initiated, otherwise the work thread waits for notification.  On completion of either the check action is re-initiated.

A *process* action [internal] executes the handler of a work item that has been marked running.  When the handler returns, atomically:
* The item running state is cleared;
* The item cancelling state is cleared;
* All processes waiting for completion of the work item are made ready.

A *drain* action [external] indicates that the queue needs to be drained to empty.  Atomically:
* If the work list is empty and the work thread is idle, return false; otherwise
* Mark the queue draining and pend on the drain waitq.

A *flush* action [external] indicates that the caller must wait until completion of a given work item should be signalled.

### Minutiae

Flush and synchronous cancel operations involve pushing a marker onto the work list immediately after whatever work item is being flushed or cancelled.

## Item States and Actions

Design requirements:
* It must be possible to synchronously cancel a non-delayable work item in the sense of [Linux cancel_work_sync](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/workqueue.html#c.cancel_work_sync).
  (If queued, remove from queue.  Otherwise block attempts to resubmit and flush.)

  Note: This differs from `flush_work` in that any attempts to resubmit the work before cancellation completes will be rejected.

* {TBD} It must be possible to asynchronously (ISR) cancel a delayable work item in the sense of [Linux cancel_delayed_work](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/workqueue.html#c.cancel_delayed_work).
  (If scheduled, abort timeout.  If queued, remove from queue.)

* It must be possible to synchronously cancel a delayable work item in the sense of [Linux cancel_delayed_work_sync](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/workqueue.html#c.cancel_delayed_work_sync).

* It must be possible to synchronously flush a non-delayable work item in the sense of [Linux flush_work](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/workqueue.html#c.flush_work). (Basically inserts a notifier in the work queue immediately after the
  work item.)

* It must be possible to synchronously flush a delayable work item in the sense of [Linux flush_delayed_work](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/workqueue.html#c.flush_delayed_work).  (If delayed, the timeout is cancelled and the item immediately queued.  Otherwise equivalent to flush_work().)


### States

There is a global work item lock that protects the flag

A work item has a *node* that allows it to be linked into work lists.

A work item has a *handler* function that is invoked when it is de-queued by a work thread.

A work item has a set of flags including:
* *delayed* if there is a timeout that will submit the item to a specific workqueue when the delay expires;
* *queued* if it is on the queue for a work thread to process;
* *running* (??) if a work thread is running its handler (this is required to ensure non-reentrancy when submitting.  It may be derived from a non-null workq pointer in the work object.)
* *cancelling* if it has been cancelled and is also running.
* *flusher* if the item is a flush marker;

An item is *owned* if it is in at least one state of delayed, queued, or cancelling.

Note that idle is the only distinct state: a work item may be simultaneously delayed, queued, and running.

### Events

A *submit* action (ISR-OK) provides an item and a workqueue.  Atomically:
* If the item is running, the provided workqueue is replaced with the workqueue running the item; then
* If the item is not queued and not cancelling, it is submitted to the workqueue.  If the submission is successful the item is marked queued.

The action result indicates whether the item was queued.

A *process* action from the work thread mutates the queued and running flags.

A *complete* action from the work thread mutates the running and cancelling flags.

A *schedule* action (ISR-OK) provides a work item, a workqueue, and a delay.  Atomically:
* If the item is not owned:
  * if the delay is zero, a submit action is initiated for the item and the workqueue; otherwise
  * a timeout is scheduled to perform a submit operation for the item and the workqueue after the delay expires
The action result indicates whether the item was owned.

A *reschedule* action (ISR-OK) provides a work item, a workqueue, and a delay. Atomically:
* if the item is delayed, the timeout is cancelled and the delayed flag is cleared;
* evaluate the body of the schedule action when the item is not owned.
The action result indicates whether the item was originally owned.

A *flush* action (thread-only) provides a work item.
* If the item is running, the calling thread blocks on the waitq for notification when the item completes.
Note: Nothing prevents scheduling or submitting the item again; the notification occurs only when then the currently running instance completes.

A *cancel* action (ISR-OK) provides a work item.  Atomically:
* If the item is delayed, its timeout is cancelled and the delayed state cleared;
* If the item is queued, it is removed from its queue and the queued state cleared;
* If the item is running, it is marked as cancelling.

A *cancel-sync* action (thread-only) provides a work item.  Atomically:
* a cancel action is executed; then
* if the item is marked cancelling a flush action is initiated.
</details>

Another attempt to respond:

The existing API *does not meet community needs*.  There is no way to precisely determine the state of any work item, nor to be informed when it's safe to shut down a work queue, nor to submit another work item without risking duplicate handling because of race conditions.

This PR provides the work queue capabilities that I believe Zephyr needs, with many desirable functional improvements, grounded on an architectural approach from Linux that's proven to be generally satisfactory.

The first milestone is whether this implementation is acceptable to the kernel folks on technical grounds.  The second milestone is whether the existing API can be implemented in terms of it without significant behavioral differences.  The third milestone is whether the new capabilities are exposed in a way that fits how applications will want to use them.

We're at the first milestone.  That's why this is in draft.

Yes, in an ideal world we would have only one workqueue implementation: there would not be a `k_work2*`, just `k_work*` with different internals and new API adjacent to the existing API.  That's a goal.  It is not yet clear that can be reached (there are very weird behaviors that application code may be depending on), but if it can, it isn't going to be accomplished by extending the existing implementation.  The data structures and state management it uses are the wrong ones; for example `k_queue` is a locked data-structure, but precise tracking of work state requires a lock with wider scope, so `k_queue` gives no benefit over `sys_slist_t`.

If we're stuck at the first milestone for more than a week it'll probably work back to the top of my queue and I'll start on checking compatibility, but for now I'm working other issues while waiting for kernel review.

The proposed path completely replaces the original implementation with a new one that precisely tracks the state of work items, allowing confirmation when one has completed and a variety of other features including flushing and draining work queues.  This precise tracking requires the use of spin locks: there's too much interaction to do it with atomics alone.

Because spin locks seem to be unsupported in usermode the usermode work queue API cannot be implemented.  We need to determine whether this is a showstopper, and what if anything should replace it.  It may be possible to replace use of spinlocks with futex for work and queues in userspace, especially if userspace doesn't need to have the API be safe for use from ISRs.  I haven't pursued that possibility.

The implementation also uses low-level kernel API like `slist` and `_wait_q` directly as its locks make higher level API like `k_queue` and `k_sem` of limited value.  This was partly done in support of making `k_work_queue` a kernel object, since having a kernel object that contained kernel objects seemed to add complexity with respect to granting access.

A few examples where userspace access to workqueue api is useful:
1. Implement blinking LEDs using system event queue rather than dedicating a thread per LED (that is put to sleep for each on/off duration) (Nordic Nrfconnect SDK Mesh  light example e.g. uses such a strategy). 
Simple to invoke LED blinking from a user thread and continue processing.
2. Rather than employing a dedicated thread and timer to process a future event such as an application protocol timeout, place on system event queue

3. Initially design an application with several ISRs offloading non-realtime processing to system event queue. When see performance degradation due to event rate or event processing duration, simple to re-architect and move a subset of the events to a dedicated user queue/processing thread. Since all manipulation of the flags must be under lock, we don't *need* the atomic API: I can use standard bitwise operations on an integral type.  But for the instantaneous capture of the state there are two options:
* Make `k_work_is_busy()` an external function call that takes the lock, captures the state, releases the lock, and returns the state.  This is expensive compared to the existing implementation using `atomic_get()`.
* Continue to use the inline atomic API to do the read, even though it wasn't used for the write. > Currently the k_work flags track some, but not all of the states that a k_delayed_work item can be in (or at least the valid multi-bit states are not explicit (e.g. are running+canceling and delayed+running valid combinations?)

Yes.  As has been stated before, a work item can be any subset of:
* busy on one queue (with or without canceling);
* pending on (the same) queue
* scheduled to run on a (possibly different) queue

simultaneously.  It can also be idle.  This maps to at least nine distinct static states, each of which can transition to one or more next states depending on the action involved and whether the action succeeds or fails.  Because the action is not atomic with the state update, we'd need to introduce transient states e.g. `IDLE` to `QUEUING` to `QUEUED` with or without `CANCEL` happening at any point in the sequence.  This causes a state explosion and a frightfully complicated transition diagram.

Doing this with atomic actions is IMO not feasible, which is why there is a lock.  This allows the parallel states to be managed mostly independently.

Note that Linux also uses a lock-plus-atomic solution to manage state for their concurrent work queue implementation, so I'm not the only one who came to this conclusion (and Linux has a significantly more powerful atomic capability it can leverage).

Most of the rest of your comments are based on the assumption that it's possible do this with atomic alone, which is unproven, but some of the responses may be helpful in understanding why things are the way they are.  If you are able to log in to github and comment directly on the code, that would help everybody see the context.  If that is not possible, we can continue with isolated fragments.

> `queue_remove_locked()` is an example where formal state transitions could reduce use of work lock. (assign different non-zero
states before and after taking the spin lock.)

IMO not feasible, see above.

> * finalize_cancel_locked() :
> clear bit **after** finding and removing from list.

I don't see how this has any impact with the current lock/semaphore implementation.  It was placed before to make clear that the work item can be re-used as soon as the thread waiting for it was released.  Clearing it after releasing the thread that needs it cancelled would be wrong if the thread started running while the bit was still set.

> Consider moving k_sem_give()  outside of iterator statement in case don’t find item on list.

Why?  If you don't find the item, there's no semaphore to give.  If you do, you're done and the loop terminates.  The current placement seems optimal.

> * submit_to_queue_locked(): should return error if delayed bit is set

A work item can't reach that function if the delayed bit is set unless somebody uses the non-delayed API on a delayable item, in which case that's their problem.  I could add an `__ASSERT()` there, if somebody's really worried about it.

> * k_work_submit_to_queue(): can completely remove this spin lock if move the line `atomic_set_bit(&work->flags, K_WORK_QUEUED_BIT);` in submit_to_queue_locked() into queue_submit_locked()

No, because `submit_to_queue_locked()` is also invoked in other contexts where the lock must be held.

> * k_work_flush() : unclear why need spin lock here, since also take one in work_flush_locked().

They're two different locks: one on the work item, one on the queue it might still be on.  This order of double-locking is documented as intentional and required.

> It may even be possible to push spin lock usage even further down in call hierarchy.

Not really; `work_flush_locked()` is also invoked from other contexts where the lock must be held.

> * work_queue_main() : unclear why need spin lock protecting atomic_clear_bit()

Because the `BUSY` flag is inspected under lock in `k_work_queue_drain` which would fault if its value changed while checking the complex condition.

issue_context.title: deep review and redesign of API for work queue functionality
issue_context.body:
As requested by @andrewboie [here](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/22826#pullrequestreview-455050386) and rephrasing [this comment](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/22826#pullrequestreview-371142029):

As demonstrated in #23132 although `k_delayed_work_cancel()` is documented to return `-EALREADY` if the work item has been *completed*, it actually returns it if the work item has already been submitted.

I'm skeptical of the whole k_work implementation.  I'm seeing at least nine distinct states for a work item that is not cancelled:
* never submitted
* delayed on timeout
* timeout expired, not yet added to queue (in `z_clock_announce()`)
* marked pending but not on queue (by `k_submit_to_queue`)
* on queue
* removed from queue (by `z_work_q_main`)
* cleared pending (by `z_work_q_main`)
* invoking handler (by `z_work_q_main`)
* complete

Most of these can't be inferred by inspecting the state.

Somebody should take the time to go through the whole k_work API and implementation and revise it so the documentation accurately describes the behavior and the functionality is useful.  By "useful" I mean that after an attempt to cancel you should always be able to tell whether the item was:

* submitted but not yet committed to processing (delayed or on queue): can be cancelled, 0
* processing (including committed to processing, not yet in handler): cannot be cancelled, now `-EINVAL`  preferably `-EINPROGRESS`
* complete (which may be indistinguishable from unsubmitted): too late to cancel, now `-EALREADY` preferably `-EINVAL`

This capability should be present whether the item is a standard work item, a delayed work item, or a pollable work item.
comments: @andrewboie @andyross I plan to start on this later this week.  If it's something you'd like done in-house at Intel instead please reply here.

review_comments: Naming: I see a "schedule **for** queue" function which is implemented in terms of a "schedule **to** queue" function, and I don't think English language prepositions have the kind of expressive power being demanded of them here.  Maybe they're just synonyms, but being different makes me afraid there's a distinction that I can't understand from the name.
Yeah.  There is/was a subtle difference at one point but rather than explain it it's easier to rename the internal function to match.  (And make it `static`, which it somehow wasn't.)
global locks like this are somewhat legacy, is it possible to move the granularity of this lock to  the individual work items, or the relevant workqueue they are on?

Unfortunately, no.  This protects the flags of individual work items across complex states checks/changes that can't be performed with a single atomic action, at times when the work item might not be associated with a queue.  Similarly it protects queue flags which have to be manipulated while the work flags are protected, and vice-versa.

I don't think you really answered my question.

> Unfortunately, no. This protects the flags of individual work items across complex states checks/changes that can't be performed with a single atomic action, at times when the work item might not be associated with a queue. 

I didn't say we leave all concurrency to the queue object. If the intention is to protect flags in work items, why not introduce a lock into the work item itself instead of having a global spinlock here? So the queue has a lock, and the work items have themselves locks, instead of a global lock for all the work items.

> Similarly it protects queue flags which have to be manipulated while the work flags are protected, and vice-versa.

You can use multiple spinlocks in a critical section as long as they are always acquired and released in the same order. Can you provide more detail on why you think this is not possible?

I can tell you from experience it is VERY bad to have the same data protected by different locks at different times. Queue flags should not be sometimes protected by the queue lock, and sometimes by the work item global lock. You're better off just using one global lock for everything if things are mixed up like this.

They aren't "mixed up like this": no specific state is protected by different locks at different times.  Some state in one domain needs to remain protected while additional state in another domain is updated.

The global work lock, as documented, protects two things:
* Mutation of the work item flags, which cannot be done solely with the atomic API due to the coarseness of available atomic actions.  The code in `submit_to_queue_locked` is an example: multiple conditions must be checked, and flag state changed only based on the results of condition-specific actions.
* The list of work items that are being cancelled

The queue lock, as documented, protects multiple things:
* the flags describing work queue state;
* the list of work items to be processed and the wait queue used to notify the work thread when that list changes;
* the list of threads waiting for the queue to drain.

As documented, the queue lock can be taken when the global work lock is already held.  This allows us to set up flags on a work item, then add it to the queue without risk of the work state changing because something else tries to cancel it.  The queue lock can also be taken independently for tasks that are specific to it---like getting the next work to process.

No other lock (including the work lock) can be taken while the queue lock is held, which is also documented.

We can't get away from having the "global" lock on the cancel list, and the work item has to be locked while the cancel list is updated.  The simplest and most clearly correct way is to have one lock that covers the list and all work items that may or may not be on it.
I know this is bike-shedding but can you move the empty line from 423 to 421 to create a neat `lock-do-unlock` code block?

Checkpatch will come at you if you try that.  It demands a newline after declarations.  Which runs afoul of our increasingly common habit of using inline declaration/initialization pairs.  I love that personally, but it's not allowed in the Linux kernel which wants classic top-of-function declaration blocks (I guess for easier manual stack estimation?  honestly I don't know why).

Maybe we should see about changing that rule...

Is this racy?  This has made a decision that it needs to block inside the lock, but releases the lock before it gets here.  Can another thread sneak in, do its own cancel of the same work item, and deadlock us here?  (Or likewise muck with the item such that this semaphore operation is wrong, maybe it'll restart, cancel again, and we'll end up stealing the notification cookie?)

I don't see how it's racy.  The notification cookie is passed in by the caller and is documented to be specific to that call, so even if multiple threads cancel the same item simultaneously each one will get its own notification.

(There was a bug, though: the notification loop incorrectly assumed each work item would appear in `pending_cancels` only once, so it stopped checking after the first match.  This has been fixed).

(probably I am missing something here...)

Could you explain to me why an external sync struct is needed? Is it possible to declare it inside this function so it exists in the stack?

It cannot be declared in this function, because it contains a node that is linked into the work queue to be processed when the requested work item completes, which may not happen until after this function returns.

It can be defined on the stack of the caller if the target platform is cache-coherent, but on some platforms it would have to be in memory accessible by other processors.

> which may not happen until after this function returns.

Honestly, to me it also seems that it will not leave this function until work is completed as it will pend on semaphore or return immediately if work was done. Given that, it seems to me that sync struct could be internal automatic variable.

Originally the motivation for `k_work_sync` was userspace access, but that's no longer relevant.  The remaining concern here is with architectures that are not cache coherent, which I understand to mean there are problems with visibility of thread stacks between processors.  We need at minimum a semaphore, and for cancel an slist node that links the semaphore into the canceling list.

If kernel folks like @dcpleung and @andyross confirm that putting such data in the thread stack won't cause problems on any architecture Zephyr needs to support then I'll refactor this.

I'll wait until this is resolved before finalizing updates.

Sorry, @carlescufi had to call me over.

The cache coherence is specific to Xtensa SMP platforms with their L1 cache enabled, which right now means the various intel_adsp devices.  The framework we decided on for managing that is that all non-stack data is by default coherent and uncached, and thus safe (there is an __incoherent linkage specifier for apps that know what they are doing).  But stacks are cached, and it's never legal to inspect another thread's stack (strictly: it's never legal to inspect the stack of a thread that has last run on another CPU).

So yeah, that means no IPC data like semaphores or or shared lists on the stack.  Where I've had to work around this, I've relied on static data mostly, or in a pinch by stealing data in the thread struct.  If it's absolutely required, we actually could write a thin layer that would allow putting manually-flushed data on the stack.  You'd have to pack it into an exclusive cache line (Xtensa has 64 bit cache lines) and carefully invalidate and flush it as needed (maybe in combination with a spinlock acquire/release?).   Cache management gets mindbending though....

OK, so that says we can't generally put the synchronization objects on the stack: they have to be provided by the caller and be in non-stack memory if the operation is going to work on Xtensa SMP.

The problem is that even though `k_work_sync` is documented as do-not-stack-allocate when `CONFIG_KERNEL_COHERENCE=y` nobody's going to pay any attention to that, so generic code where the caller allocates the thing on the stack is still going to break on Xtensa SMP.  So what we have now may not work right, even though there's just such a case in `test_smp_running_cancel()` in `tests/kernel/qorkq/work` which hasn't shown failures.  Maybe that's due to `arch_cohere_stacks()` flushing the cache on context switch, so it just works as long as the processor running the work queue thread context switches?

There was a similar issue with k_poll addressed in dadc6643e45cde165d474874632674c2f0f185c2 so we could instead put a `k_work_sync` object in a union with the `struct _poller` in the thread memory.

At this point unless `arch_cohere_stacks()` makes this irrelevant I'm inclined to try that.  @andyross do you see a problem with it?  Including the increase in per-thread memory requirements (`struct z_work_flusher` is rather bigger than `struct _poller`.)

FWIW: if you want to enforce a rule like that, I don't see it as too onerous.  KERNEL_COHERENCE is a separate mode for a reason; most apps aren't going to want to follow those rules.  You can check pointers at runtime with `arch_mem_coherent()` and assert on them if you need to catch mistakes.

The problem then is that you need to make sure that any test code we have in-tree uses only coherent data.
I've gone with the document-and-assert approach, so the API will work in the general case.
deadcode?
why do you have this condition ? I mean what is the difference if the work is in or not in the list ?

If the work item we're waiting for is in list, the work item that notifies of completion must *follow* that item.  If it's not in the list, then the work item has already completed, and the notification item can be run immediately.

This is really more of a misfeature in the thread name API, but this construction is racy.  Starting the thread with K_NO_WAIT and then setting the name means that there is a moment while the work queue thread is running with no name.  Pass K_FOREVER and start it after this call using `k_thread_start()`.
Thanks; done.

This may introduce a priority inversion. Thread that cancels the work, regardless of the priority, will be bound by priority of work thread.
In general integrator may not be willing or be in need to have work thread of high priority, while using it to maintain timeouts (and so willing to sync cancel them) for some high priority thread.
Considering what the thread does it is not a problem as long as work thread is coop.

I'm not clear what can be done about this.  As you say, if the caller wants to wait for confirmation the work has been canceled then that confirmation can be delayed until the work queue releases the item.  If the caller is high priority, maybe it should cancel asynchronously first and if the cancellation didn't complete in that call issue a synchronous cancel from another context.

Do you want some text in the documentation, e.g. that `_sync()` operations on work items may be blocked waiting for the work queue thread to release them?  I would think that would be fairly obvious once the question is posed.

I don't think that can be handled easily.
Guess the best way to go is to add a warning in doc - if that is critical one can always elevate the priority of the work thread manually.
what happens if the state of the K_WORK_QUEUED or K_WORK_RUNNING flags changes by preemption or another CPU in between the check of the flags here, and the logic which acts upon it?
How could that happen?  It's protected by the work lock.
why flushing cannot be used here? i cannot catch the difference.
The state of cancelling is associated with the work item.  The state of flushing is not.

These details are all uniformly scheduler-specific.  What's the value of trying to document them in a header like this?  The only code that can productively use this is going to be effectively part of the scheduler internals anyway.  Note (mentioned elsewhere too) that holding the scheduler lock means that virtually the entirety of the Zephyr process state API is going to be unusable to this callback!

Wouldn't it be simpler to just call out to whatever functions you want and discriminate via an argument here?  The callback abstraction seems like a guaranteed footgun for someone in the future.
i wonder if it is possible to add a protection against case when it is called from the context of work queue thread as that will deadlock.

That concern also applies to `k_work_{,delayable_}cancel_sync`.

The documented behavior is that the call doesn't return until the work has completed (cancellation).  If the thread that's invoking the operation is the thread that will signal completion of the operation, yes, it'll deadlock.  Just as could happen with any semaphore both given and taken by the same thread.

We could change the API so that it can also return an error code saying that the cancel/flush operation was rejected, if this is a serious concern.

Otherwise I think the answer is "Don't do that".  I've added another note to the documentation.
FWIW: digging up and down through this file, this is AFAICT the **only** piece of data that the global lock is protecting.  Everything else is inside a queue.
? It's also protecting all non-atomic RMW operations on `flags` and associated state in each work item.
This loop is digging through an slist looking for a specific item to delete.  Virtually always, that means you should be using a dlist instead, where deletion is O(1).
This was wrong, because though `sys_slist_remove()` is O(1) the prev-node parameter was incorrect.  That's been corrected; is this OK now?  It's an idiom used multiple other places.

That call is O(1), but you're literally looping over the list right here.  And AFAICT, the only purpose of this list is to store an unordered set of things that never gets looped over or inspected in any way except to remove elements.  Unless there's a really clear reason for why you can't spend the extra word of storage in the node, an slist is just the wrong data structure here.

But I have to iterate over the list to identify the items that need to be removed (by checking for canceller records that reference the completed work item), and while doing so it's trivial to delete them as I encounter them.  What does switching to dlist get us?

i have some doubts regarding this functionality. Work was delayed for some reason, now when we want to sync until it is finished we are also getting it rescheduled to immediate execution. It seems to me that it would be good to have an option to choose whether i want to reschedule or wait until it is executed at scheduled time.

Perhaps, but this is the behavior of the corresponding Linux API.  This behaves "as expected" when the work item is both scheduled and submitted: on flush the work is completely done, not potentially completing multiple times.

The infrastructure to handle "wait until it's scheduled, and then wait until it's done" could get complicated, and it's not obvious that's useful.
is it necessary to read that under lock? there is no api to change it after initialization.
It's necessary to read flags under lock.  Rather than read it once on entry and dedicate stack space for the cached value it made more sense to re-read it here.
`flusher` has to be uninitialized but it  is coming from `&sync->flusher` in `k_work_flush` that does not say anything about it
Yes; `sync` is provided by the caller, and is intended to be an uninitialized object, probably held on the stack.  I've updated the documentation to make that more clear.
couldn't return value be used to avoid calling `cancel_async_locked` when timeout was cancelled?

No, because the item might have been both scheduled and submitted.  `unschedule_locked` can only remove the scheduled submission; if it's already submitted or running it still needs to be cancelled normally.
why not passing priority in the same config structure?

You always have to provide a priority; you don't always have to provide any other customization.  If we want to make the queue config structure required, we could move all the parameters except the queue pointer itself into it.
I feel it may be useful to indicate canceling with a separate code.

Possibly.  It's not needed internally, so to be useful it'd have to propagate up to `k_work_submit_to_queue()`, where it would allow distinguishing cancelling from queue is draining or plugged.

Generally if a module chooses to use the cancel feature it's the responsibility of that module to not make use of the work item until the cancellation has resolved (completed or not necessary).  So attempting to submit an item after attempting to cancel it without waiting for the cancellation to complete is rather like the pervasive misuse of the existing API where the cancellation result isn't even checked.

How badly do you want this?

We can go without it. I was thinking about a case when one would like (for some reason) to know if interrupt is racing with a timeout. I would add it if it's cheap to do as it would be pain to do it later (in case it would be useful for somebody).

If you think it takes too much effort, please ignore the comment. I have given a green tick already :)
